newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong democratic reforms defended and denounced.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong democratic reforms defended and denounced.

text.p: Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten said on Friday he saw no need to curb civil liberties after China takes over the territory, but a senior Asian statesman said the governor's democratic initiaties had to be rolled back.
"What still hasn't been addressed is the question of why these changes (to civil liberties laws) are necessary in the first place," Patten told reporters.

"I've been governor in Hong Kong for five happy years and I've never felt there was any demonstration taking place in Hong Kong -- and there have been a lot while I've been here -- which threatened the national security of China or the national security of the United Kingdom."

Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa announced on Thursday a partial retreat from his plan to amend laws on political funding and public demonstrations after Britain hands back the territory to China on July 1.
The new versions narrow a ban on foreign political funding and moderate limits on the right to protest. Nonetheless, opponents say the proposals are unchanged on essentials.

Singapore's Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew said Tung had to roll back some of Patten's democratic reforms in order to keep China's confidence and to maintain the civil and economic liberties Hong Kong had before Patten's arrival.

"He can protect and maintain the freedoms and liberties which Hong Kong enjoyed before Governor Patten attempted to enlarge them, provided this is to preserve Hong Kong's system, and not to change the system in Guangdong province, or worse, the PRC (China)," Lee said in a lecture in Tokyo.
Tung has told interviewers he numbers Lee among his heroes, along with the late Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping and former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher.
In addition to presiding over an easing of draconian colonial securities laws, Patten introduced electoral reforms that produced Hong Kong's first fully-elected legislature.

That legislature is to be replaced on July 1 with a provisional council appointed by a 400-member China-backed committee and the new body is expected to endorse the proposed tightening of civil liberties ordinances.

Lee, one of Asia's foremost exponents of firm government rule, pointedly excluded Patten's democratic reforms from what he listed as Britain's positive legacy in Hong Kong: sound administration and legal framework and financial discipline.
"Patten's political agenda has provided a stick for foreign lobby groups to beat China with," said Lee, who led the former British colony of Singapore to independence in the early 1960s.
Patten was toasted by Democratic Party legislators who are due to lose their seats on July 1 and threw an informal farewell dinner for him at a sea food restaurant.
The party won 19 seats in the September 1995 polls, making it the largest bloc in the 60-seat legislature, but it refused to participate in the provisional council which it labels illegal.
In another sign of the impending handover, the British garrison packed its radio station into a shipping container.

The British Forces Broadcasting Service, which has broadcast in Hong Kong since 1971, left its studios at military headquarters but plans to stay on the air until the last minute from a mobile studio in a 20-foot container.
"I'm sure there'll be something in the last hours," said Commodore Peter Melson, chief of staff in Hong Kong. "It's not something we'll let go easily, not after so long."
